newsitem.title: ITALY: Buba eyed Europe, currencies before Aug repo cut.
newsitem.headline: Buba eyed Europe, currencies before Aug repo cut.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the central bank decided to make its latest cut in its key repurchase rate after considering the impact of such a move on the rest of Europe.
The Bundesbank, when it lowered the repo rate to 3.0 percent from 3.30 percent in late August, cited an appropriate favourable international environment as part of its reasoning.

Asked in a news conference here what that meant, Tietmeyer said, "We looked to see whether the decision would have a negative impact on the situation in Europe. We saw it would be more favourable in Europe to have a decline and that there would be no negative impact."
"Secondly we looked to see whether it would have a negative impact on exchange rates.
"Clearly we never follow a monetary policy which is mainly looking to the exchange rate but of course we take into account what could be the exchange rate effect," he said.
Germany's discount rate has stood 2.50 percent and its Lombard rate at 4.50 percent since April this year.
Tietmeyer said present interest rates were in line with the economic situation in Germany and the situation in general in Europe.
However he reiterated this did not meant the end of the road for the current phase of monetary policy and the bank would continue monitoring the situation.
Asked about the high level of German unemployment, which is at 10.3 percent, Tietmeyer said the reasons for the unemployment rate were outside the monetary area.

But he said: "Investors are looking at long term rates. You know that in Germany at least more or less 70 or 80 percent of all activities are financed on longer term rates. Longer term rates are much more important than short term rates for economic activities."
